_comment: Class ceilings the build enforces over dose_ranges (pipeline/build/dose_gates.py). For a class whose members are dosed in micrograms, a ladder tier above `max_tier_mg` is a unit slip or a copied error rather than a dose, and the row is deleted unless it carries a citation or comes from an exempt source. `exempt_substances` names the members the class premise does not hold for, each with its own citation — a ceiling is a statement about a class, so a member that is genuinely dosed in milligrams is an exemption, never a reason to raise the ceiling for everyone. Every deletion is listed in data/snapshots/dose-gate-report.md. Keyed by class_contexts.slug.

gates.reason: fentanyl is dosed in tens of micrograms and no anilidopiperidine in human use is more than ~100× weaker (PMID 40721041 ranks six analogs within a decade of fentanyl in vivo); a tier above 2 mg is a milligram written for a microgram

the nitro-/alkoxy-substituted nitazenes in circulation are orders of magnitude above morphine per milligram — etonitazene ~1,000× and metonitazene ~100× morphine in the original potency series, isotonitazene ~500× (EMCDDA risk assessment report on isotonitazene, doi:10.2810/107576, Table 3) — so for them a tier above 2 mg is not a dose

exempt_substances.reason: clonitazene is the member the class premise does not hold for: it was given to humans by mouth in tens of milligrams. The same EMCDDA report records single oral doses of 100 mg as "about one-third to one-fifth as potent as morphine sulfate (20 and 30 mg) and roughly equivalent to codeine", and a 35-day pain-treatment trial using repeated 50 mg oral doses, against a relative oral potency of 5 in mice. A milligram-scale oral ladder for it is therefore in range, not a unit slip
